subject: Creativity
title: Morphological Analysis: Mapping Possibility Space
description: A micro-lesson that makes Morphological Analysis: Mapping Possibility Space usable.

hook.text: Fritz Zwicky mapped every possible jet engine design in a grid. The result: engines nobody had imagined became obvious.

buildup.text: Morphological analysis breaks a problem into independent dimensions, then lists options for each dimension in a matrix.

discovery.text: Combining one option from each dimension creates a unique solution. A 5×5×5 matrix yields 125 combinations.

twist.text: Zwicky, an astrophysicist, used this method to predict neutron stars in 1934 — decades before they were observed.

climax.text: The Swedish military uses morphological analysis for strategic planning.

punchline.text: List the dimensions. Combine the options. Discover what nobody imagined.

quiz.question: What does morphological analysis map?
options: All possible combinations across problem dimensions

details.summary: Morphological analysis breaks a problem into its independent dimensions, lists options for each dimension, then systematically combines them. This creates a matrix of all possible solutions, many of which are combinations no one would think of intuitively.
details.whyItMatters: Morphological analysis guarantees exhaustive exploration of a solution space. It prevents the common mistake of fixating on one approach when hundreds of unexplored combinations exist.
takeaways: Problems are decomposed into independent variable dimensions
Each dimension has multiple possible values or options
Systematic combination reveals non-obvious solution candidates

faq.question: How do you set up a morphological analysis?
faq.answer: List the key parameters of your problem as columns. Under each column, list all possible values for that parameter. Then create combinations by selecting one value from each column. Evaluate each combination for feasibility and novelty.

faq.question: Is morphological analysis practical for complex problems?
faq.answer: For problems with many dimensions, the number of combinations can be enormous. In practice, you narrow the dimensions to the most critical three to five and eliminate obviously impractical combinations early to keep the process manageable.
